intro: This guide leads a group of teenagers, aged about 13 to 18, through “The Imitation of Christ (For Teens)” in thirteen weeks, one chapter a week. Thomas à Kempis wrote his little booklets in the 1420s for the young novices in his monastery, so this is a book that was written for young people from the start: blunt, kind and very practical about gossip, temptation, friendship, criticism and peace. It suits a youth group, a homeschool or a small group of any size.

Each session takes about 30 to 40 minutes. Open by saying the memory verse together. Read the chapter, either aloud together or beforehand at home if your group prefers to come ready. Talk through the chapter’s three questions, which come with answers to help you guide the conversation. Do the activity, which takes about ten minutes. Close by praying the chapter’s prayer, or your own.

To prepare, read the chapter yourself during the week and think about which line will land hardest with your group; most activities need only paper and pens. Thomas wrote in strong monastery language, and the teen edition already softens a few places, so follow its lead: we are not asked to go looking for suffering or to give up friends, and the chapters on temptation, other people’s words and death need a gentle hand. Never ask anyone to name a sin, a struggle or a hurt aloud; keep personal reflection private. If a teen mentions bullying, self-harm or anything that is hurting them, thank them for telling you and make sure they get help from a trusted adult. In the last week, be ready to talk calmly about death, and to say simply that Christians from different churches understand Communion differently.

weeks.summary: We meet Thomas à Kempis, who joined the monastery of Mount St Agnes at about nineteen, stayed for about seventy years, and wrote short booklets of advice for its young novices that became The Imitation of Christ. His opening idea is that if you want to see clearly, you imitate Jesus, and he borrows Ecclesiastes to call everything else “vanity”: money, admiration and endless cravings are bubbles that never fill us up. The big idea: only God can fill the emptiness that more seeing and hearing never will.

memory_verse.text: Vanity of vanities, says the Preacher, vanity of vanities! All is vanity.

activity.title: Bubbles and Treasure
steps: Give each person a sheet of paper and ask them to list, on their own, ten things people their age chase to feel full: things to own, ways to be noticed, ways to fill time.
In pairs, sort the list into two columns: things that last and things that fade, like a bubble.
Come back together and ask: which ‘bubbles’ are hardest to see through, and why?
Read Thomas’s line aloud, “Vanity of vanities and all is vanity, except to love God and serve Him alone,” and ask each person to write down privately one bubble they will give a rest this week.

weeks.summary: Thomas, a man who spent his life with books, warns that knowledge without love and humility can puff us up, and that you can win every argument about God and still not know him. He says that on the day of judgment we will be asked not what we have read but what we have done, and that the Bible should be read with humility, simplicity and faith. The big idea: being wise means doing what God says, not just knowing a lot about him.

memory_verse.text: But be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves.

activity.title: Know It or Do It?
steps: Choose three short, familiar verses that ask us to do something, such as Micah 6:8, Matthew 5:44 and Philippians 2:3.
Split into small groups and give each group one verse to read slowly together.
Ask each group to answer one question only: “What does this ask me to do?” and to name one specific, ordinary way a teenager could do it this week.
Share the answers, then ask each person to choose one action and write it down for themselves to try before next week.

weeks.summary: Thomas admits he often wished he had kept quiet, and asks why we gossip when we so seldom part “without a troubled conscience.” He does not condemn all talk, praising good conversation about God, but he warns against curiosity about other people’s business, echoing Jesus’ words to Peter: “What is that to thee? follow thou me.” The big idea: speak to build people up, and leave other people’s business with God while you follow Jesus yourself.

memory_verse.text: Know this, my beloved brothers: let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger.

activity.title: Does This Build Anyone Up?
activity.materials: Slips of paper with short scenarios
steps: Before the session, write six short scenarios about group-chat or lunch-table talk, for example: “Someone posts a screenshot of a friend’s private message” or “The group starts discussing why a classmate was absent.” Use made-up situations only.
Read each scenario aloud and ask the group to decide together: does joining in build anyone up, tear someone down, or just fill the silence?
For each one, ask what a person could say or do instead: change the subject, stay quiet, or say something kind.
Finish by asking everyone to remember Thomas’s test for the week: before talking about someone who isn’t there, ask, “Does this build anyone up?”

weeks.summary: Thomas talks about the monk’s cell, a small plain room for being quiet with God, and says that if we cut out idle talk and gossip we will find enough time to pray. Being alone with God can feel boring at first, but he promises that if you keep returning, your quiet place will become “a special friend and a very great comfort.” The big idea: Jesus invites us to shut the door and meet with our Father in secret, and it gets easier with practice.

memory_verse.text: But when you pray, go into your room and shut the door and pray to your Father who is in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you.

activity.title: Two Minutes of Quiet
steps: Explain that the group is going to practise what Thomas describes: put phones out of reach and sit quietly for two minutes. Anyone may close their eyes or simply look at a window.
Afterwards, ask: what did the silence feel like? Restless, awkward, peaceful? There are no wrong answers.
Talk about where each person’s ‘cell’ could be this week: a bedroom, a bench, a walk.
Ask everyone to write down for themselves a time and a place for ten quiet minutes with God each day this week.

weeks.summary: Thomas says no one is so holy that they are never tempted, and that temptation can humble and strengthen us: “Fire tempers iron and temptation steels the just.” He traces how temptation grows from a mere thought to imagination, pleasure and consent, and urges us to shut the door while it is still knocking, to seek counsel, and to be gentle with others who are tempted. The big idea: fight temptation at its first knock, and remember God always makes a way out.

memory_verse.text: No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation he will also provide the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it.

activity.title: The First Knock
steps: Draw Thomas’s five steps on a board or sheet: thought, imagination, pleasure, delight, consent.
Using an ordinary, low-stakes example everyone shares, such as wanting to copy homework or staying up scrolling, ask the group to describe what each step might look like.
Ask: at which step is it easiest to say no? Talk about practical ways to ‘shut the door’ at the first knock.
Give everyone a moment to write privately, for themselves only, one temptation they face and a simple plan for its first knock. Nobody shares what they wrote.

weeks.summary: Thomas warns that we often judge others wrongly and want them perfect while excusing ourselves: “We wish them to be severely corrected, yet we will not correct ourselves.” He urges patience, because “you also have many a fault which others must endure,” while making clear that if someone is hurting you, you should tell an adult who can help. The big idea: God made us imperfect together so that we would learn to bear one another’s burdens.

memory_verse.text: Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.

activity.title: My Annoying Habits
steps: Ask the group to call out, light-heartedly, the kinds of habits that tend to annoy people in families, teams or classes, without naming anyone.
Now turn it round: ask each person to write down privately two or three habits of their own that other people probably have to put up with.

Discuss together: why is it so much easier to see other people’s faults than our own? Read Thomas’s question, “If you cannot make yourself what you would wish to be, how can you bend others to your will?”
Ask everyone to think of one person they find hard to be patient with and to pray for them by name each day this week.

weeks.summary: Writing as Christ speaking to a disciple, Thomas says not to let our peace depend on what people say, because their opinion “does not make you different from what you are,” and it is impossible to please everyone. He asks whether harsh words could pluck one hair from your head, while also saying that if criticism is true we should use it to change. The chapter is clear that bullying or threats must be told to a trusted adult. The big idea: God knows the truth about you, so other people’s words do not get the final say.

memory_verse.text: The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe.

activity.title: True or False?
steps: Read out a few made-up comments a teenager might hear, some fair and some unfair, such as “You never finish anything” or “You’re only friends with them because they’re popular.”
For each one, ask the group how they could tell whether it contains any truth, and what Thomas would say to do in each case: change, or let it go.
Give each person a card and ask them to write privately one thing said about them that keeps going round their head, then mark it ‘true’ or ‘false’ for themselves. They keep the card.
Close by reading together: “God, you know the truth about me.”

weeks.summary: Thomas points to Jesus as the friend who will not leave us, saying that when Jesus is near all is well, and that “It is a great art to know how to converse with Jesus.” He is not against other friendships; his point is order, because when Jesus is first we can love our other friends better and survive it when they let us down. When Jesus feels far away, Thomas says to wait and trust, “for after winter comes summer.” The big idea: Jesus is the friend who stays, and putting him first makes every other friendship stronger.

memory_verse.text: No longer do I call you servants, for the servant does not know what his master is doing; but I have called you friends, for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you.

activity.title: What Makes a Good Friend?
activity.materials: A large sheet of paper and markers
steps: As a group, brainstorm the qualities of a really good friend and write them on the sheet.
Go through the list and ask: which of these does Jesus show in the Gospels? Ask for a story or example for some of them.
Talk about how friendships with Jesus and with others grow in the same way: time together and honest conversation.
Ask everyone to decide privately on one friend to thank God for this week, and one moment each day to talk to Jesus about their day.

weeks.summary: In “The Royal Road of the Holy Cross,” Thomas says some suffering comes to everyone and that we cannot escape it by running away, “for wherever you go you take yourself with you.” If we carry the cross willingly, “it will carry and lead you,” while fighting it makes it heavier; the teen edition adds that we should never seek out suffering and should always get help for anything that is hurting us. The big idea: when hard things come, we do not carry them alone, because Jesus carried his cross first.

memory_verse.text: And he said to all, “If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me.”

activity.title: Carry or Drag?
steps: Ask a volunteer to drag the bag across the room by one strap, then to pick it up and carry it properly on their back. Ask them which was easier.
Read Thomas’s line: “If you carry the cross willingly, it will carry and lead you to the desired goal.” Discuss what it might mean to ‘carry’ a hard thing rather than ‘drag’ it.
Talk about the difference between hard things we cannot change and things that need help: illness, pain, or someone hurting us should always be told to a trusted adult.
Give everyone a quiet moment to name, privately, one hard thing they cannot change, and to ask Jesus to help them carry it with him this week.

weeks.summary: In one of the book’s most famous passages, the disciple breaks into a song about love: it “makes every difficulty easy,” bears burdens without being weighed down, and is “never self-seeking.” Thomas says this love is born of God and rests only in God, and the teen edition reminds readers that it begins with God loving us first. The big idea: real love comes from God, and the moment love becomes all about me, it stops being love.

memory_verse.text: We love because he first loved us.

activity.title: Love Is…
steps: Read 1 Corinthians 13:4–7 aloud together.
Read it again, this time putting the name “Jesus” in place of “love,” and ask the group what changes when they hear it that way.
In pairs, pick one of Thomas’s lines, such as “Love feels no burden” or “Love is never self-seeking,” and think of an everyday example of it from home, school or sport.
Ask each person to write down privately one person they will love in a practical, unselfish way this week, and how.

weeks.summary: Christ tells the discouraged disciple, “You are a man, not God. You are flesh, not an angel,” so falling is human and the point is not to stay down. Thomas tells of an anxious man who heard God say, “Do now what you would do then and you will be quite secure,” and suggests uprooting just one bad habit each year. The big idea: God does not expect us never to fall; he helps us get up and follow him faithfully today.

memory_verse.text: For the righteous falls seven times and rises again, but the wicked stumble in times of calamity.

activity.title: One Habit, One Step
steps: Read aloud the story of the anxious man in the church and God’s answer, then discuss: why do we worry about the far future more than we act on today?
As a group, list some common habits teenagers might want to work on, such as procrastinating, snapping at family or too much screen time, without anyone sharing their own.
Ask each person to choose privately one habit for this year and write one small step for this week.
Teach the group Thomas’s quick prayer for when they slip: “I’m not an angel, Lord. Help me up.”

weeks.summary: Thomas says we would have much peace if we did not concern ourselves with what others say and do, and in Book III Christ gives four short rules: do the will of others rather than your own, choose to have less, take the last place, and want God’s will above all. The disciple notices that whenever he feels troubled, he has drifted from this teaching. The big idea: much of our lost peace comes from pushing to win, to have and to be first.

memory_verse.text: You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you, because he trusts in you.

activity.title: Rank the Four
steps: Write the four rules where everyone can see them, put into everyday words: let others have their way, don’t grab for more, don’t fight for first, want God’s will most.
Ask each person to rank the four privately from easiest to hardest for them.
Without asking anyone to reveal their ranking, discuss which rule the group thinks is hardest for teenagers today, and why.
Ask: what is the difference between these habits and being a doormat? Then encourage everyone to check the four each evening this week.

weeks.summary: Thomas, writing for young people, urges them not to count on “later” but to become now the person they want to be at the end: “How happy and prudent is he who tries now in life to be what he wants to be found in death.” He says we need two things above all, “food and light,” which he saw in Communion and in God’s word, and the chapter notes that Christians understand Communion differently. Thomas died at Mount St Agnes in July 1471. The big idea: follow Jesus today, and live now the way you would want to be found at the end.

memory_verse.text: So teach us to number our days that we may get a heart of wisdom.

activity.title: Letter to My Future Self
steps: Read Thomas’s line about trying “now in life to be what he wants to be found in death,” and ask the group what it might mean for someone their age.
Give each person paper and ask them to write a short private letter to their future self: the kind of follower of Jesus they hope to be when they are old.
Ask them to add one thing they will start doing this week to become that person.
Have everyone seal their letter in an envelope and write a date on it, perhaps a year from now, to open it. Nobody reads anyone else’s.
